_about: Verified law file for AI Lawyer (consumer complaints, India). The AI may ONLY use entries marked status=verified. Every verified entry links to an official government source (India Code, Parliament, Ministry of Consumer Affairs, National Consumer Helpline, NALSA). Last checked: 6 November 2026.
scope: Consumer problems in India: refund not received, defective product, poor service, online shopping (e-commerce) complaints.
out_of_scope: claims above Rs 50 lakh (refer to a lawyer)

entries.title: The main consumer law
entries.plain: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 is the main consumer law in India. It came into force in July 2020 and replaced the 1986 Act. It sets up consumer commissions at district, state and national level to settle consumer disputes.

entries.title: Who counts as a consumer
entries.plain: You are a consumer if you bought goods or used a service and paid for it (fully, partly, or promised to pay), including buying online, by teleshopping, direct selling or multi-level marketing. The person using it with the buyer's permission also counts. You are NOT a consumer if you bought it to resell or for a commercial purpose; but buying something to earn your own living by self-employment is not a commercial purpose.

entries.title: Which commission to go to (by amount paid)
entries.law: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 read with Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021
entries.plain: The commission depends on the value of goods or services paid (not the compensation claimed). District Commission: up to Rs 50 lakh. State Commission: above Rs 50 lakh up to Rs 2 crore. National Commission: above Rs 2 crore.

entries.title: Which city's commission (place of filing)
entries.plain: You can file at the District Commission of the place where you live or work for gain, OR where the seller/service provider lives, does business or has a branch office, OR where the problem (cause of action) arose, fully or partly.

entries.title: How long the commission should take
entries.plain: Every complaint should be decided as quickly as possible, and the commission should try to decide it within about three months. In practice it often takes longer.

entries.title: Deadline to file a complaint
entries.plain: A complaint must be filed within two years from the date the problem (cause of action) arose. A late complaint can still be accepted if you show a sufficient reason for the delay, and the commission records why it accepts it.

entries.title: Online shopping: company must reply within set time
entries.plain: Every e-commerce platform must have a grievance officer whose contact details are shown on the platform. The officer must acknowledge your complaint within 48 hours and resolve it within one month of receiving it.

entries.title: Free pre-court route: National Consumer Helpline
entries.law: Department of Consumer Affairs, Government of India (not a law section)
entries.plain: Before going to a commission, you can register a complaint free with the National Consumer Helpline: call 1915 (8 AM to 8 PM) or 1800-11-4000, send an SMS or WhatsApp to 8800001915, or use the NCH app, the UMANG app or the website consumerhelpline.gov.in. It works in 17 languages.

entries.title: Filing a case online: e-Jagriti
entries.law: Department of Consumer Affairs / consumer commissions portal (not a law section)
entries.plain: Since 1 January 2025, consumer complaints can be filed online on e-Jagriti, which brings the older systems (including e-Daakhil) into one platform. You can submit documents and pay the fee online, from anywhere.

entries.title: Free legal help
entries.plain: Some people can get a free lawyer through their District Legal Services Authority (DLSA), including: women and children, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, persons with disabilities, industrial workers, victims of disasters or trafficking, people in custody, and people whose yearly income is below the limit set by their state.
